name: Lichen simplex chronicus (vulval)
aliases: squamous cell hyperplasia of the vulva

reference.source: Standard gynaecology and vulval dermatology textbook guidance
clinicalPearls: Vulval lichen simplex chronicus is a reactive skin change produced by a persistent itch-scratch cycle rather than a primary disease in its own right
The dominant symptom is relentless itch, often worse at night and during stress, which drives rubbing and scratching that in turn thickens the skin and perpetuates the itch
Chronic scratching produces lichenification, seen as thickened, leathery skin with accentuated skin markings, often with excoriations and variable pigment change
It commonly arises on a background of an underlying trigger such as atopic or contact dermatitis, a pre-existing dermatosis, or environmental irritants, which should be sought and treated
Diagnosis is usually clinical, but biopsy is indicated when the appearance is atypical, unilateral, or fails to respond, to exclude a specific dermatosis or neoplasia

Management aims to break the itch-scratch cycle with generic measures: avoiding irritants, restoring the skin barrier with emollients, potent topical anti-inflammatory treatment for flares, and addressing nocturnal scratching
Identifying and treating any underlying dermatosis or allergen is essential to prevent relapse
Persistent, non-resolving, or ulcerated areas require re-biopsy because chronic vulval skin disease can rarely harbour intraepithelial neoplasia
reference.pathophysiology: Lichen simplex chronicus is the end result of repeated mechanical trauma to the skin from chronic rubbing and scratching. An initial pruritic stimulus, whether an underlying dermatosis, irritant contact, dryness, or psychological stress, provokes scratching that damages the epidermis and stimulates further itch through nerve and inflammatory mediators, establishing a self-sustaining itch-scratch cycle. Persistent trauma leads to epidermal thickening (acanthosis and hyperkeratosis) and dermal changes that clinically appear as lichenification. The condition is therefore secondary and reactive, and lasting improvement depends on interrupting the cycle and removing the provoking cause.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination for lichenification, excoriation, and features of an underlying dermatosis
Vulval biopsy for atypical, unilateral, or treatment-resistant lesions
Skin swabs or scrapings to exclude candidal or dermatophyte infection
Patch testing where allergic contact dermatitis is suspected
Assessment for atopy and systemic causes of pruritus
redFlags: A persistent unilateral plaque, ulcer, or nodule requiring biopsy to exclude neoplasia
Failure to respond to appropriate anti-inflammatory treatment
Progressive architectural change suggesting lichen sclerosus rather than simple lichenification
reference.prognosis: The condition usually improves well once the itch-scratch cycle is broken and any underlying trigger is treated, but it is prone to relapse if irritants recur or scratching resumes, so ongoing skin care is often needed.
pitfalls: Treating the lichenification without identifying and correcting the underlying itch trigger, leading to relapse
Missing an underlying lichen sclerosus or intraepithelial neoplasia by not biopsying atypical or resistant areas
Under-treating with weak topical preparations so the itch-scratch cycle continues
Ignoring nocturnal scratching, which sustains the process
Overlooking contact allergens or irritants from hygiene products
references: Gynaecology guidance on vulval skin disorders
management: Identify and treat the underlying trigger, such as atopic or contact dermatitis, another dermatosis, infection or an irritant
Restore the skin barrier with emollients and soap substitutes and eliminate identified irritants
Apply potent topical corticosteroids to settle flares of lichenification and inflammation
Break the itch-scratch cycle with sedating antihistamines and measures to reduce nocturnal scratching
Consider topical calcineurin inhibitors as a steroid-sparing maintenance option
Address psychological stress that aggravates scratching
Biopsy atypical, unilateral or treatment-resistant lesions to exclude a specific dermatosis or neoplasia, and patch test where contact allergy is suspected
